problem.statement_vernacular: Knee pain on the right side

subjective.vernacular: Where exactly in the knee does it hurt, and how would you describe the pain — sharp, aching, burning, or something else?
subjective.why_it_matters: Medial versus lateral versus diffuse pain, and character such as aching versus sharp versus burning, helps distinguish osteoarthritis from meniscal tear, ligamentous injury, or referred pain.

subjective.vernacular: When did the knee pain start, and did it come on gradually or suddenly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Gradual insidious onset over months to years favors osteoarthritis or chronic overuse, while sudden onset suggests acute injury such as meniscal tear or ligament rupture.

subjective.vernacular: What makes the pain worse — stairs, prolonged sitting, twisting, or walking — and what makes it better?
subjective.why_it_matters: Pain worse with weight-bearing and activity relieved by rest is characteristic of osteoarthritis, while pain at rest or at night raises concern for inflammatory arthritis, infection, or neoplasm.

subjective.vernacular: When you wake up, is the knee stiff, and if so how long does that stiffness last before it loosens up?
subjective.why_it_matters: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes supports osteoarthritis, whereas stiffness lasting more than 45–60 minutes suggests inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Does the knee ever lock up, catch, click, or give way unexpectedly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Locking or true catching suggests a loose body or meniscal tear, while giving way indicates possible ligamentous instability or patellofemoral dysfunction.

subjective.vernacular: Has the knee been visibly swollen, and if so does swelling come on quickly after injury or gradually over hours?
subjective.why_it_matters: Rapid hemarthrosis within hours of injury points to ligamentous tear or fracture, while slow effusion developing over 24 hours is more consistent with meniscal injury or inflammatory arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever injured this knee before, had surgery on it, or been told you had a torn ligament or cartilage?
subjective.why_it_matters: Prior ACL tear, meniscectomy, or intra-articular fracture significantly increases lifetime risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis in the affected knee.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have pain, swelling, or stiffness in other joints, skin rashes, eye problems, or mouth sores?
subjective.why_it_matters: Polyarticular involvement, rashes, uveitis, or oral ulcers raise the possibility of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or other systemic inflammatory conditions.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever been told you have gout or crystal deposits in a joint, or had sudden attacks of intense joint pain and redness that resolved on their own?
subjective.why_it_matters: A history of crystalline arthropathy or classic acute attacks makes gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease a candidate explanation for episodic knee pain.

subjective.vernacular: How far can you walk before the pain stops you, and what daily activities — like getting up from a chair, climbing stairs, or dressing — have become difficult?
subjective.why_it_matters: Quantifying functional limitation establishes severity baseline and guides whether conservative care, rehabilitation, or surgical referral is most appropriate.

subjective.vernacular: Have you had fever, unexpected weight loss, night sweats, or fatigue alongside the knee pain?
subjective.why_it_matters: Constitutional symptoms accompanying joint pain raise concern for septic arthritis, systemic inflammatory disease, or malignancy involving bone or synovium.

subjective.term: Body weight and recent weight change
subjective.vernacular: What is your current weight, and have you gained or lost significant weight recently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis progression, and recent weight gain can accelerate joint loading symptoms.

objective.term: Standing alignment — varus or valgus deformity
objective.vernacular: Assessment of whether the knee bows outward (bow-legged) or inward (knock-kneed) when standing

objective.term: Range of motion — active and passive
objective.vernacular: How far the knee can bend and straighten, both on the patient's own effort and when the examiner moves it
Fluid swelling inside the knee joint detected by palpation or ballottement of the patella

objective.term: Joint line tenderness — medial and lateral
objective.vernacular: Whether pressing along the inner or outer joint line reproduces pain
Special maneuvers that stress the meniscus to see if they reproduce a click or pain

objective.term: Ligamentous stability testing (Lachman, anterior/posterior drawer, varus/valgus stress)
objective.vernacular: Examiner tests whether the knee moves abnormally in ways that suggest torn ligaments

objective.term: Patellofemoral provocation (Clarke sign, patellar grind, patellar apprehension)
objective.vernacular: Tests that press or move the kneecap to see if it causes pain or a grinding sensation

objective.term: Weight-bearing plain radiographs of right knee — AP, lateral, and sunrise views
objective.vernacular: Standard X-rays of the knee taken while standing to assess joint space, bone spurs, and alignment
Calculated weight-to-height ratio used to assess obesity as a contributing factor
Blood test measuring uric acid level to evaluate for gout
Blood markers of inflammation that rise with inflammatory arthritis or infection
Blood tests that help identify rheumatoid arthritis

objective.term: Synovial fluid analysis — if effusion present
objective.vernacular: Lab examination of fluid drawn from inside the knee joint, looking at cell count, crystals, and culture

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Wear-and-tear breakdown of the knee joint cartilage that develops over time
not_yet_testable: s-002 (onset and duration — not yet gathered)
o-002 (range of motion — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Osteoarthritis is the most prevalent cause of knee pain in adults over 45; characterized by gradual onset, activity-related pain, crepitus, bony enlargement, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No record data exist yet; probability reflects strong population prior for knee pain in general adult presentation labeled probable OA.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Without management, joint damage and functional loss can progress and become difficult to reverse, ultimately requiring joint replacement.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tear in the rubbery cartilage pads (menisci) that cushion the knee
not_yet_testable: o-004 (joint line tenderness — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Meniscal tears are common causes of knee pain at all ages; degenerative tears are particularly prevalent over age 40 and may coexist with or be mistaken for osteoarthritis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot distinguish from OA without physical exam maneuvers and imaging; probability held conservatively pending workup.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: An untreated symptomatic tear can cause persistent pain, swelling, and accelerate cartilage loss if a displaced fragment causes mechanical damage.

assessment_candidates.term: Crystalline arthropathy — gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Joint pain caused by uric acid crystals (gout) or calcium crystals (pseudogout) depositing inside the knee
not_yet_testable: o-010 (serum uric acid — not yet ordered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Gout and CPPD can present with acute or chronic knee pain and swelling; CPPD is particularly common in the knee of older adults and can mimic OA on X-ray with chondrocalcinosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot rule in or out without serum uric acid, synovial fluid analysis, and targeted history; included because it is treatable and commonly missed.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Recurrent crystal attacks damage joint cartilage over time and cause significant pain episodes; gout is fully manageable with the right treatment.

assessment_candidates.term: Inflammatory arthritis — rheumatoid or seronegative spondyloarthropathy
assessment_candidates.vernacular: An immune system attack on the knee joint lining, as seen in rheumatoid arthritis or related conditions
assessment_candidates.basis: Inflammatory arthritides can present as monoarticular knee involvement; missing this diagnosis leads to progressive joint destruction that is preventable with DMARDs.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Probability is low for isolated knee presentation but rises substantially if prolonged morning stiffness, bilateral involvement, or elevated inflammatory markers are found.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated inflammatory arthritis causes irreversible joint erosion and disability that may not be recoverable even with later treatment.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain originating from the kneecap and its underlying cartilage, often felt at the front of the knee
not_yet_testable: s-003 (aggravating factors such as stair climbing — not yet gathered)
o-007 (patellar provocation tests — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Patellofemoral syndrome is a common diagnosis across a wide age range; characterized by anterior knee pain worsened by stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without knowing pain location and patellar exam; probability will shift substantially once location is clarified.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Generally not destructive but causes significant functional limitation; responds well to targeted physical therapy when identified correctly.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A bacterial or other microbial infection inside the knee joint requiring urgent treatment
not_yet_testable: s-011 (fever and constitutional symptoms — not yet gathered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Septic arthritis is uncommon in chronic knee pain but must not be missed; risk rises with recent joint injection, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, or skin breakdown near joint.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Listed because the consequence of missing it is catastrophic; probability considered very low for a chronic pain presentation but cannot be formally excluded without key data.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and can be fatal from systemic sepsis; it is a medical emergency.

assessment_candidates.term: Bone tumor or metastatic disease involving distal femur or proximal tibia
assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tumor growing in the bone near the knee, either originating there or spreading from cancer elsewhere
not_yet_testable: s-003 (rest pain or night pain — not yet gathered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Malignant bone lesions near the knee can mimic arthritis; rest pain, night pain, and constitutional symptoms are red-flag features; plain X-ray is first screening tool.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Rare in the absence of known malignancy but severity mandates inclusion; probability will drop sharply if X-ray shows only degenerative changes.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: A missed bone malignancy is potentially fatal; early identification changes prognosis dramatically.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.term: Weight-bearing knee radiographs — AP, lateral, sunrise views
plan_options.vernacular: Standing X-rays of the right knee to look for joint space narrowing, bone spurs, and alignment
plan_options.basis: ACR/AAFP guidelines recommend weight-bearing plain films as the first imaging study for suspected knee osteoarthritis; Kellgren-Lawrence grading guides management.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (physician, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Structured physiotherapy referral with quadriceps and hip strengthening program
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to physical therapy focused on strengthening the muscles around the knee to reduce joint load
plan_options.basis: OARSI and NICE guidelines rank exercise therapy as first-line treatment for knee OA with strong evidence for pain reduction and functional improvement.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; carried out by physical therapist

plan_options.term: Weight management counseling and referral
plan_options.vernacular: Guidance and support to reduce body weight to lower mechanical load on the knee
plan_options.basis: Each kilogram of weight loss reduces knee joint compressive force by approximately 4 kg; weight loss combined with exercise is the most effective conservative intervention for knee OA.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician, dietitian, obesity medicine specialist

plan_options.term: Analgesic trial — acetaminophen or topical NSAID first line
plan_options.vernacular: A trial of pain relievers, starting with acetaminophen or a gel/cream NSAID applied to the knee
plan_options.basis: OARSI 2019 guidelines recommend topical NSAIDs as first-line pharmacotherapy for knee OA; oral NSAIDs are effective but carry GI and cardiovascular risk requiring individual assessment.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; patient can self-initiate OTC acetaminophen

plan_options.term: MRI of right knee — if meniscal tear suspected after exam
plan_options.vernacular: An MRI scan of the knee to look for meniscal tears, ligament injuries, and cartilage damage if physical exam raises suspicion
plan_options.basis: MRI is the gold standard for soft tissue knee pathology with sensitivity >90% for meniscal tears; indicated when clinical exam findings suggest tear that would alter management.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (physician, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Serum uric acid and synovial fluid aspiration for crystal analysis
plan_options.vernacular: Blood test for uric acid level and, if fluid is present, drawing fluid from the knee joint to look for crystals under the microscope
plan_options.basis: Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test for crystalline arthropathy; serum uric acid provides supporting evidence; both are necessary to distinguish gout from CPPD.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician for blood test; physician or trained clinician for joint aspiration

plan_options.term: Inflammatory arthritis serologies — ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP
plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests to screen for rheumatoid arthritis and measure the degree of inflammation in the body
plan_options.basis: Anti-CCP has >95% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis; elevated CRP/ESR in the context of prolonged morning stiffness and polyarthritis should prompt rheumatology referral.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician

plan_options.term: Urgent joint aspiration with synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count — if septic arthritis suspected
plan_options.vernacular: Emergency drawing of fluid from the knee joint to look for infection if fever, warmth, and rapid onset swelling are present
plan_options.basis: Septic arthritis requires same-day joint aspiration for definitive diagnosis and immediate antibiotic therapy; delay increases risk of irreversible joint destruction and systemic sepsis.
plan_options.who_can_act: Emergency physician or orthopedic surgeon — urgent referral

plan_options.term: Orthopedic surgery referral for consideration of intra-articular corticosteroid injection or surgical options
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to a joint specialist if conservative measures fail, to discuss steroid injections into the knee or surgery such as joint replacement
plan_options.basis: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection provides short-term pain relief in knee OA; total knee arthroplasty is indicated for severe OA with functional limitation refractory to conservative care.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician initiates referral; orthopedic surgeon performs

problem.statement_vernacular: Knee pain on the right side

subjective.vernacular: Where exactly in the knee does it hurt, and what does the pain feel like — sharp, dull, aching, burning?
subjective.why_it_matters: Medial joint-line aching suggests osteoarthritis or meniscal pathology; anterior pain points toward patellofemoral syndrome; sharp or burning pain raises neuropathic or referred causes.

subjective.vernacular: When did the knee pain start, and has it been coming and going or constant?
subjective.why_it_matters: Gradual onset over months to years favors osteoarthritis or chronic meniscal tear; acute onset after trauma favors ligament or meniscal injury; episodic pain with swelling raises crystal arthropathy.

subjective.vernacular: Does the knee lock up, catch, give way, or feel unstable when you walk or climb stairs?
subjective.why_it_matters: Locking or catching suggests a displaced meniscal tear or loose body; giving way implicates ligamentous instability or patellofemoral dysfunction.

subjective.vernacular: When you wake up, how long does knee stiffness last before it loosens up?
subjective.why_it_matters: Stiffness under 30 minutes favors osteoarthritis; prolonged morning stiffness over 45–60 minutes raises inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Has the knee been swollen or puffy at any point, and if so, did it come on suddenly or build up slowly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Rapid effusion after minor stress suggests hemarthrosis or acute crystal attack; gradual swelling is more consistent with osteoarthritis or chronic synovitis.

subjective.vernacular: What makes the pain worse — stairs, sitting a long time, kneeling — and what helps it feel better?
subjective.why_it_matters: Pain worsening with prolonged sitting and stair descent points to patellofemoral syndrome; pain worsening with weight-bearing and relieved by rest is typical of osteoarthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Has taking ibuprofen helped the knee pain, and if so, how much?
subjective.why_it_matters: Good NSAID response supports inflammatory or crystalline arthropathy; partial response is consistent with osteoarthritis; poor response raises neuropathic, referred, or structural mechanical causes.

subjective.vernacular: Has there been any injury to the right knee — a fall, twist, sports injury, or accident — ever?
subjective.why_it_matters: Prior trauma predisposes to post-traumatic osteoarthritis and meniscal or ligament damage that may now be symptomatic.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have pain or swelling in other joints, skin rashes, mouth sores, eye redness, or recent infection?
subjective.why_it_matters: Polyarthritis with systemic features raises rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or reactive arthritis rather than isolated degenerative disease.

subjective.vernacular: How much does the knee pain limit what you can do day-to-day — walking, climbing stairs, sleeping?
subjective.why_it_matters: Mobility is already listed as a patient-reported challenge, making functional impact central to goal-setting and urgency of intervention.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Wear-and-tear breakdown of the cartilage and bone in the main hinge part of the right knee joint
not_yet_testable: o-004 (joint line tenderness — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: Most common cause of unilateral knee pain in adults; prior overweight diagnosis and age 38 are risk factors; PCOS is associated with metabolic syndrome and accelerated joint degeneration.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Leading possibility but cannot confirm without X-ray showing joint space narrowing and physical exam findings; all subjective and exam data still absent.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If untreated, can progressively limit walking and independence, but usually manageable with therapy, medication, and in some cases joint replacement.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tear in the shock-absorbing cartilage pads inside the knee, which can happen gradually with age or suddenly after a twist
not_yet_testable: o-004 (joint line tenderness — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: Degenerative meniscal tears are common in adults over 35 and frequently co-exist with or mimic early osteoarthritis; prior weight excess and PCOS-associated metabolic load increase susceptibility.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot distinguish from osteoarthritis without clinical exam maneuvers and ideally MRI; mechanical symptoms would raise this significantly.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Can cause significant pain and mechanical limitation; often managed without surgery but may require arthroscopic intervention if locking or instability is present.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain coming from the underside of the kneecap where it tracks against the thigh bone — common in people who are less active or have alignment issues
not_yet_testable: o-003 (inspection for alignment — not yet done)
o-006 (range of motion — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: Common cause of anterior knee pain in adults; mobility limitation and sedentary challenges documented in shared care plan raise risk; occurs independently of radiographic osteoarthritis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Plausible but requires anterior pain character and positive patellofemoral provocation tests to support; cannot assess without exam.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Rarely dangerous but can be disabling; usually responds well to physiotherapy and activity modification.

assessment_candidates.term: Gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Crystal deposits in the knee joint that cause sudden, severe pain and swelling — gout is uric acid crystals; pseudogout is calcium crystals
not_yet_testable: o-010 (serum uric acid — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: PCOS is associated with insulin resistance and hyperuricemia; pseudogout is more common in middle-aged women and the knee is the most commonly affected joint.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Low probability without history of episodic acute attacks or elevated uric acid, but must be excluded given PCOS metabolic context.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Acute attacks are very painful and disabling but treatable; chronic tophaceous gout can cause joint destruction if uncontrolled.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: An immune system disorder causing ongoing joint inflammation — rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions can start in a single joint
not_yet_testable: s-004 (morning stiffness duration — not yet gathered)
s-009 (polyarthritis or systemic features — not yet gathered)
o-012 (RF and anti-CCP — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Rheumatoid arthritis prevalence is higher in women and can present as monoarthritis early; PCOS and autoimmune conditions share immune dysregulation pathways.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Unlikely as presenting diagnosis without systemic or polyarticular features, but high-severity if missed and allowed to progress.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated inflammatory arthritis can cause permanent joint destruction and systemic organ involvement over years.

assessment_candidates.term: Referred pain from hip or lumbar spine
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain felt in the knee that is actually coming from the hip joint or a pinched nerve in the lower back
not_yet_testable: o-006 (knee range of motion — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: L3–L4 nerve root compression and hip pathology commonly refer pain to the knee; diagnosis of exclusion when intrinsic knee findings are absent on exam.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without a full hip and lumbar spine exam; normal knee exam would make this more likely.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If the true source (spine or hip) is missed, the knee will not improve with local treatment and the underlying condition may worsen.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A bone growth — either a tumor starting in the bone or cancer that has spread there — causing pain near the knee
not_yet_testable: o-003 (inspection for mass — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: Prior hospitalization with pathology specimen, echocardiogram, and chest X-ray in 2023 raises unresolved questions about a prior serious diagnosis; severe unexplained bone pain warrants exclusion of malignancy.

assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Malignant bone involvement, if present and undetected, could be life-threatening without timely diagnosis and treatment.

problem.statement_vernacular: Knee pain on the right side

subjective.vernacular: How long have you had this knee pain, and did it start gradually or after a specific injury or event?

subjective.vernacular: When you wake up, is your knee stiff? If so, how long does the stiffness last — less than 30 minutes, or longer?
subjective.why_it_matters: Stiffness under 30 minutes suggests osteoarthritis; prolonged stiffness over 45–60 minutes raises concern for inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Does your knee ever lock up, catch, or give way suddenly while you are walking or moving?
subjective.why_it_matters: Locking or catching suggests meniscal tear or loose body; giving way points to ligamentous instability or patellar subluxation.

subjective.vernacular: What makes the pain worse — stairs, sitting, standing up, or activity — and what makes it better?
subjective.why_it_matters: Pain worsened by activity and relieved by rest is typical of osteoarthritis; pain at rest or at night raises concern for inflammatory arthritis or malignancy.

subjective.vernacular: Has your knee ever been swollen or felt full of fluid? If so, was it sudden or gradual?

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Wear-and-tear breakdown of the cartilage inside the right knee joint
assessment_candidates.basis: Osteoarthritis is the most common cause of knee pain in adults; weight and female sex are known risk factors. The clinical label 'probable osteoarthritis' in the problem statement reflects working assumption, not confirmed diagnosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No imaging, physical exam findings, or detailed symptom history have been gathered; probability is a prior estimate based on prevalence and demographics.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Can cause progressive loss of mobility and chronic pain, but rarely life-threatening; functional disability can worsen significantly without management.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tear in the cartilage cushion between the knee bones, which can cause pain, catching, and swelling
assessment_candidates.basis: Meniscal tears are common in middle-aged adults, can occur without significant trauma, and may coexist with or be mistaken for osteoarthritis; prevalence increases with age and prior injury.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot be assessed without physical exam and imaging; prior knee injury history is unknown.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Can cause persistent pain and mechanical dysfunction; degrades quality of life and may require surgical repair if severe.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Joint pain caused by crystals (uric acid for gout, calcium for pseudogout) depositing inside the knee
assessment_candidates.basis: Gout and pseudogout are common in middle-aged adults and frequently affect the knee; they are often missed without synovial fluid analysis or uric acid testing.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No metabolic labs or fluid analysis available; episodic pain pattern is a key differentiator that has not yet been established.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Recurrent attacks can damage joints permanently over time; acute episodes can be severely painful and disabling.

assessment_candidates.term: Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: An immune system attack on the joint lining causing chronic inflammation, pain, and joint damage
assessment_candidates.basis: Rheumatoid arthritis has a female predominance and peak incidence in the 40s–60s; psoriatic arthritis can present asymmetrically including isolated knee involvement; neither can be excluded without labs and exam.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No inflammatory markers, autoimmune serology, or polyarticular symptom history gathered; this remains a meaningful possibility that treatment-as-osteoarthritis would miss.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated inflammatory arthritis causes progressive, irreversible joint destruction and systemic organ complications.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain at the front of the knee behind the kneecap, often made worse by stairs, squatting, or sitting
assessment_candidates.basis: Common in active and overweight adults; more prevalent in females; often coexists with or is confused with early osteoarthritis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Pain location has not been established; this diagnosis rests on anterior pain pattern and patellar exam findings not yet obtained.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Causes chronic pain and functional limitation but does not cause permanent joint damage when managed appropriately.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Bacterial infection inside the knee joint — a medical emergency
assessment_candidates.basis: Septic arthritis is uncommon but must be excluded in any acute hot swollen joint; delay in diagnosis leads to rapid cartilage destruction and systemic sepsis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No fever history, systemic symptoms, or exam findings reported; this is a low-probability but high-stakes diagnosis that must remain on the list until a hot joint is formally excluded.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Can destroy the knee joint within days and cause life-threatening sepsis if not treated urgently with drainage and antibiotics.

assessment_candidates.term: Referred pain from hip or lumbar spine
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain that feels like it is coming from the knee but is actually originating from the hip joint or lower back
not_yet_testable: s-005 (relation to back or hip movement)
o-008 (hip or lumbar imaging if indicated)
assessment_candidates.basis: Hip osteoarthritis and L3–L4 radiculopathy classically refer pain to the anterior thigh and knee; misattributing hip pathology to the knee is a recognized clinical pitfall.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Hip exam and neurological assessment of the lower extremity have not been performed; this must be considered before attributing knee pain to intra-articular disease.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If the true source is the hip or spine, knee-targeted treatment will fail and the underlying condition will progress untreated.

plan_options.term: Weight-bearing right knee radiograph (AP, lateral, sunrise views)
plan_options.vernacular: X-ray of the right knee taken while standing up, which is the standard first imaging step for suspected knee osteoarthritis
plan_options.basis: ACR and OARSI guidelines recommend weight-bearing radiographs as the first-line imaging for knee osteoarthritis; standing views reveal joint space narrowing not visible on supine films.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (MD, DO, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Structured knee physical examination
plan_options.vernacular: A full exam of the right knee including inspection, palpation for joint line tenderness, range of motion, and stability tests
plan_options.basis: Physical examination is essential to characterize the problem and guide differential diagnosis before or alongside imaging.

plan_options.term: Structured exercise program and physiotherapy referral
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to physiotherapy for a supervised knee strengthening and range-of-motion program
plan_options.basis: Strong evidence (NICE, ACR) supports exercise as first-line treatment for knee osteoarthritis; quadriceps strengthening reduces pain and improves function.

plan_options.term: Analgesic optimization — acetaminophen trial or topical NSAID
plan_options.vernacular: Discuss safer pain relief options such as regular acetaminophen or a topical anti-inflammatory gel applied to the knee, given existing ibuprofen use
plan_options.basis: ACR 2019 guidelines recommend topical NSAIDs as preferred over oral NSAIDs for knee OA; acetaminophen has fewer GI/renal/cardiovascular risks than oral ibuprofen for long-term use.

plan_options.term: Serum uric acid measurement
plan_options.vernacular: A blood test to check the uric acid level and help rule in or out gout as a cause of knee pain
plan_options.basis: Serum uric acid is a useful screening tool for gout, though it can be normal during acute attacks; used in conjunction with clinical assessment.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (MD, DO, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Inflammatory arthritis serological screen (ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP)

plan_options.basis: Recommended when inflammatory arthritis cannot be excluded clinically; abnormal results warrant rheumatology referral.

plan_options.term: Urgent arthrocentesis if hot swollen joint present

problem.statement_vernacular: Knee pain on the right side

subjective.vernacular: Where exactly in the knee does it hurt, and how would you describe the pain — sharp, aching, burning, or something else?
subjective.why_it_matters: Medial versus lateral versus diffuse pain, and character such as aching versus sharp versus burning, helps distinguish osteoarthritis from meniscal tear, ligamentous injury, or referred pain.

subjective.vernacular: When did the knee pain start, and did it come on gradually or suddenly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Gradual insidious onset over months to years favors osteoarthritis or chronic overuse, while sudden onset suggests acute injury such as meniscal tear or ligament rupture.

subjective.vernacular: What makes the pain worse — stairs, prolonged sitting, twisting, or walking — and what makes it better?
subjective.why_it_matters: Pain worse with weight-bearing and activity relieved by rest is characteristic of osteoarthritis, while pain at rest or at night raises concern for inflammatory arthritis, infection, or neoplasm.

subjective.vernacular: When you wake up, is the knee stiff, and if so how long does that stiffness last before it loosens up?
subjective.why_it_matters: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes supports osteoarthritis, whereas stiffness lasting more than 45–60 minutes suggests inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Does the knee ever lock up, catch, click, or give way unexpectedly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Locking or true catching suggests a loose body or meniscal tear, while giving way indicates possible ligamentous instability or patellofemoral dysfunction.

subjective.vernacular: Has the knee been visibly swollen, and if so does swelling come on quickly after injury or gradually over hours?
subjective.why_it_matters: Rapid hemarthrosis within hours of injury points to ligamentous tear or fracture, while slow effusion developing over 24 hours is more consistent with meniscal injury or inflammatory arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever injured this knee before, had surgery on it, or been told you had a torn ligament or cartilage?
subjective.why_it_matters: Prior ACL tear, meniscectomy, or intra-articular fracture significantly increases lifetime risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis in the affected knee.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have pain, swelling, or stiffness in other joints, skin rashes, eye problems, or mouth sores?
subjective.why_it_matters: Polyarticular involvement, rashes, uveitis, or oral ulcers raise the possibility of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or other systemic inflammatory conditions.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever been told you have gout or crystal deposits in a joint, or had sudden attacks of intense joint pain and redness that resolved on their own?
subjective.why_it_matters: A history of crystalline arthropathy or classic acute attacks makes gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease a candidate explanation for episodic knee pain.

subjective.vernacular: How far can you walk before the pain stops you, and what daily activities — like getting up from a chair, climbing stairs, or dressing — have become difficult?
subjective.why_it_matters: Quantifying functional limitation establishes severity baseline and guides whether conservative care, rehabilitation, or surgical referral is most appropriate.

subjective.vernacular: Have you had fever, unexpected weight loss, night sweats, or fatigue alongside the knee pain?
subjective.why_it_matters: Constitutional symptoms accompanying joint pain raise concern for septic arthritis, systemic inflammatory disease, or malignancy involving bone or synovium.

subjective.term: Body weight and recent weight change
subjective.vernacular: What is your current weight, and have you gained or lost significant weight recently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis progression, and recent weight gain can accelerate joint loading symptoms.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Wear-and-tear breakdown of the knee joint cartilage that develops over time
not_yet_testable: s-002 (onset and duration — not yet gathered)
o-002 (range of motion — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Osteoarthritis is the most prevalent cause of knee pain in adults over 45; characterized by gradual onset, activity-related pain, crepitus, bony enlargement, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No record data exist yet; probability reflects strong population prior for knee pain in general adult presentation labeled probable OA. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Without management, joint damage and functional loss can progress and become difficult to reverse, ultimately requiring joint replacement.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tear in the rubbery cartilage pads (menisci) that cushion the knee
not_yet_testable: o-004 (joint line tenderness — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Meniscal tears are common causes of knee pain at all ages; degenerative tears are particularly prevalent over age 40 and may coexist with or be mistaken for osteoarthritis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot distinguish from OA without physical exam maneuvers and imaging; probability held conservatively pending workup. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: An untreated symptomatic tear can cause persistent pain, swelling, and accelerate cartilage loss if a displaced fragment causes mechanical damage.

assessment_candidates.term: Crystalline arthropathy — gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Joint pain caused by uric acid crystals (gout) or calcium crystals (pseudogout) depositing inside the knee
not_yet_testable: o-010 (serum uric acid — not yet ordered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Gout and CPPD can present with acute or chronic knee pain and swelling; CPPD is particularly common in the knee of older adults and can mimic OA on X-ray with chondrocalcinosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot rule in or out without serum uric acid, synovial fluid analysis, and targeted history; included because it is treatable and commonly missed. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Recurrent crystal attacks damage joint cartilage over time and cause significant pain episodes; gout is fully manageable with the right treatment.

assessment_candidates.term: Inflammatory arthritis — rheumatoid or seronegative spondyloarthropathy
assessment_candidates.vernacular: An immune system attack on the knee joint lining, as seen in rheumatoid arthritis or related conditions
assessment_candidates.basis: Inflammatory arthritides can present as monoarticular knee involvement; missing this diagnosis leads to progressive joint destruction that is preventable with DMARDs.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Probability is low for isolated knee presentation but rises substantially if prolonged morning stiffness, bilateral involvement, or elevated inflammatory markers are found. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated inflammatory arthritis causes irreversible joint erosion and disability that may not be recoverable even with later treatment.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain originating from the kneecap and its underlying cartilage, often felt at the front of the knee
not_yet_testable: s-003 (aggravating factors such as stair climbing — not yet gathered)
o-007 (patellar provocation tests — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Patellofemoral syndrome is a common diagnosis across a wide age range; characterized by anterior knee pain worsened by stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without knowing pain location and patellar exam; probability will shift substantially once location is clarified. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Generally not destructive but causes significant functional limitation; responds well to targeted physical therapy when identified correctly.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A bacterial or other microbial infection inside the knee joint requiring urgent treatment
not_yet_testable: s-011 (fever and constitutional symptoms — not yet gathered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Septic arthritis is uncommon in chronic knee pain but must not be missed; risk rises with recent joint injection, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, or skin breakdown near joint.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Listed because the consequence of missing it is catastrophic; probability considered very low for a chronic pain presentation but cannot be formally excluded without key data. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and can be fatal from systemic sepsis; it is a medical emergency.

assessment_candidates.term: Bone tumor or metastatic disease involving distal femur or proximal tibia
assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tumor growing in the bone near the knee, either originating there or spreading from cancer elsewhere
not_yet_testable: s-003 (rest pain or night pain — not yet gathered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Malignant bone lesions near the knee can mimic arthritis; rest pain, night pain, and constitutional symptoms are red-flag features; plain X-ray is first screening tool.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Rare in the absence of known malignancy but severity mandates inclusion; probability will drop sharply if X-ray shows only degenerative changes. No new entries received on 2026-07-10; estimate unchanged.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: A missed bone malignancy is potentially fatal; early identification changes prognosis dramatically.

plan_options.term: Weight-bearing knee radiographs — AP, lateral, sunrise views
plan_options.vernacular: Standing X-rays of the right knee to look for joint space narrowing, bone spurs, and alignment
plan_options.basis: ACR/AAFP guidelines recommend weight-bearing plain films as the first imaging study for suspected knee osteoarthritis; Kellgren-Lawrence grading guides management.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (physician, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Structured physiotherapy referral with quadriceps and hip strengthening program
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to physical therapy focused on strengthening the muscles around the knee to reduce joint load
plan_options.basis: OARSI and NICE guidelines rank exercise therapy as first-line treatment for knee OA with strong evidence for pain reduction and functional improvement.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; carried out by physical therapist

plan_options.term: Weight management counseling and referral
plan_options.vernacular: Guidance and support to reduce body weight to lower mechanical load on the knee
plan_options.basis: Each kilogram of weight loss reduces knee joint compressive force by approximately 4 kg; weight loss combined with exercise is the most effective conservative intervention for knee OA.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician, dietitian, obesity medicine specialist

plan_options.term: Analgesic trial — acetaminophen or topical NSAID first line
plan_options.vernacular: A trial of pain relievers, starting with acetaminophen or a gel/cream NSAID applied to the knee
plan_options.basis: OARSI 2019 guidelines recommend topical NSAIDs as first-line pharmacotherapy for knee OA; oral NSAIDs are effective but carry GI and cardiovascular risk requiring individual assessment.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; patient can self-initiate OTC acetaminophen

plan_options.term: MRI of right knee — if meniscal tear suspected after exam
plan_options.vernacular: An MRI scan of the knee to look for meniscal tears, ligament injuries, and cartilage damage if physical exam raises suspicion
plan_options.basis: MRI is the gold standard for soft tissue knee pathology with sensitivity >90% for meniscal tears; indicated when clinical exam findings suggest tear that would alter management.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (physician, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Serum uric acid and synovial fluid aspiration for crystal analysis
plan_options.vernacular: Blood test for uric acid level and, if fluid is present, drawing fluid from the knee joint to look for crystals under the microscope
plan_options.basis: Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test for crystalline arthropathy; serum uric acid provides supporting evidence; both are necessary to distinguish gout from CPPD.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician for blood test; physician or trained clinician for joint aspiration

plan_options.term: Inflammatory arthritis serologies — ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP
plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests to screen for rheumatoid arthritis and measure the degree of inflammation in the body
plan_options.basis: Anti-CCP has >95% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis; elevated CRP/ESR in the context of prolonged morning stiffness and polyarthritis should prompt rheumatology referral.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician

plan_options.term: Urgent joint aspiration with synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count — if septic arthritis suspected
plan_options.vernacular: Emergency drawing of fluid from the knee joint to look for infection if fever, warmth, and rapid onset swelling are present
plan_options.basis: Septic arthritis requires same-day joint aspiration for definitive diagnosis and immediate antibiotic therapy; delay increases risk of irreversible joint destruction and systemic sepsis.
plan_options.who_can_act: Emergency physician or orthopedic surgeon — urgent referral

plan_options.term: Orthopedic surgery referral for consideration of intra-articular corticosteroid injection or surgical options
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to a joint specialist if conservative measures fail, to discuss steroid injections into the knee or surgery such as joint replacement
plan_options.basis: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection provides short-term pain relief in knee OA; total knee arthroplasty is indicated for severe OA with functional limitation refractory to conservative care.
